name: Kate
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_quote: The first syllable of a word always carries the heaviest stress (indicated by ´), and weaker stresses (`) occur on the alternate following syllables. In three syllable words, however, the weak stress on the third syllable is often omitted. Examples are: há.ta 'road', ká.ro.rac 'cloud' and sá.ma.rì.e.kac 'he exerted himself'.

tone_statements.citation: Bradshaw, Joel. 2016. Papuan Kâte and Austronesian Jabêm: Long contact, little convergence. Language & Linguistics in Melanesia (Journal of the Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea, ISSN 0023-1959) 34(1): 59-76.
tone_statements.quote: In sum, the Kâte and Jabêm vowel systems have not converged. (However, Sio’s six-vowel system matches that of Kâte.) Jabêm developed phonemic tone for internal reasons, but no tonal distinctions are found in Kâte. Kâte’s very distinctive coarticulated labiovelar stops have no counterpart in Jabêm (nor in Sio, contra Dempwolff). The only notable area of possible phonological convergence seems to be in canonical syllable shapes.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is present verbatim (modulo scanned spacing) in the PL-C41 scan we hold at p. xx under 'Stress Placement', with the pp. xxi-xxii continuation also matching. (2) The classification 'fixed-strict', rule 10/100/1010/10100.. (initial primary, alternating secondaries, optional loss of the third-syllable secondary in trisyllables) is exactly what McElhanon states, including his remark that diphthongs count as single vowels for stress. The source is a professional linguist's phonological sketch (1976/77) by the leading Huon-languages specialist, and it is the same source StressTyp2 and Gordon 2002 rely on. (3) Against Glottolog's bibliography there is no reference grammar, phonology monograph or instrumental study of Kâte; the two plausible modern candidates (McElhanon 1974 Kivung; Suter 2018 thesis) were downloaded and are silent on stress placement. sources.note: In the section comparing Kâte and Jabêm phonology the author states that Jabêm (and Bukawa) have high/low tone but that 'no tonal distinctions are found in Kâte' (p. 65) and, in the conclusion, that 'Jabêm's tonal distinctions have not penetrated into Kâte' (p. 73). An explicit not-tonal statement for Kâte by an Austronesianist working from the published Kâte descriptions (second-hand for Kâte, first-hand for Jabêm); no statement about Kâte stress.
